content.text: A useful weekly trading review takes about 30 minutes and answers five questions: what were the numbers, did I follow my rules, which setups worked, what behavior repeated, and what is the one thing I'll change next week. The goal isn't to relive every trade. It's to find the pattern your daily reviews are too close to see.

Do it at the same time every week, when the market is closed. Saturday morning or Sunday afternoon both work. Below is the template we use, with the numbers that matter most if you trade a prop firm account.

rows: Direction over several weeks, not one week
Win rate and average win / average loss
A falling average win often means cutting winners early
Above 1.0 is profitable; compare to your own average
Best day as % of net profit
If one day carries most of the profit, check your firm's rule
Shrinking buffer means smaller size next week

content.text: Write the numbers before you look at individual trades. Seeing the totals first keeps one dramatic trade from dominating the review.
List your rules and mark each day yes or no. This is the most honest part of the review.
Then compare: what was your P&L on days you followed every rule versus days you didn't? For many traders, this single comparison is the most persuasive data point in their journal.

items: Group trades by setup tag. Note count, win rate and net result for each.
Pick the best trade of the week and the worst. For each, write what you saw, why you entered and how you managed it.
Don't change a setup based on one week. Look at the running total over 20 to 30 trades of that setup.
Planned vs impulsive: how many impulsive trades, and what did they cost?
After losses: did you re-enter quickly? Did size increase?
Emotions: which emotion tag shows up on your worst trades? Tired, bored, frustrated?
Time of day: are your losses concentrated in a specific window?

content.text: Part 5: One Change for Next Week (5 minutes)

Write exactly one change, make it specific, and make it measurable. "Be more disciplined" isn't a change. "No trades after 11:30 AM ET" or "15-minute pause after every loss" is. Next week's review starts by checking whether you kept it.

items: Week of: ___ | Account: ___ | Net P&L: ___ | Trades: ___
Win rate: ___ | Avg win / avg loss: ___ | Profit factor: ___
Best day as % of net profit: ___ | Distance to drawdown floor: ___
Rule-compliant days: ___ of 5 | P&L on compliant days vs other days: ___ / ___
Best setup this week: ___ | Worst setup: ___
Did I keep last week's change? Yes / No

faqItems.q: How do you do a weekly trading review?
faqItems.a: Review five things in order: the numbers (P&L, trades, win rate, profit factor), rule compliance by day, setup performance, behavior patterns like impulsive trades, and one specific change for next week.

faqItems.q: How long should a weekly trading review take?
faqItems.a: About 30 minutes is enough if you log trades daily. If you don't, the review takes longer and is less accurate, because you've lost the context of each trade.

faqItems.q: What metrics should I track every week?
faqItems.a: Net P&L after commissions, number of trades, win rate, average win and loss, profit factor, best day as a share of profit, and distance to your drawdown floor if you trade a prop firm account.

faqItems.q: Should I change my strategy after a bad week?
faqItems.a: Usually not. One week is too small a sample. Look at results over 20 to 30 trades per setup, and change one thing at a time.
